summary: Extends IPv6 stateless address autoconfiguration so an address can use randomly generated, changing identifiers instead of one based on a hardware address. This makes it harder to track a device by its address. It is on the standards track. It was replaced by RFC 4941.

eli5.summary: Wearing the same name tag everywhere makes you easy to follow. This lets a computer change its tag often. A newer document later replaced it.

questions: how to stop ipv6 address tracking
how do ipv6 privacy extensions work
why do ipv6 addresses track devices
subtitle: Generating temporary IPv6 addresses to prevent device tracking

tldr.problem: IPv6 addresses contain a permanently unique interface identifier that allows trackers to identify the same device across different networks and locations.
tldr.mechanism: Devices generate temporary addresses with randomized interface identifiers that change periodically, making it harder to correlate different addresses to the same node.
tldr.outcome: Addresses change from hours to days, reducing the feasibility of tracking a device by its IPv6 address. RFC 4941 replaced this standard.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
IPv6 uses stateless address autoconfiguration, where devices generate their own addresses without needing a DHCP server. Each address combines a network prefix with an interface identifier. On devices with an IEEE identifier (such as a MAC address), that identifier is typically embedded in the address, making the address unique and consistent across all networks.

This means a single device gets the same interface identifier no matter where it connects, creating a privacy risk: an attacker can track the device across different locations and times by recognizing that interface identifier.
sections.eli5: When you get an address in IPv6, part of it is always the same for your device. That makes it easy to track you. This document fixes that.

sections.title: The Privacy Problem
sections.content:
The concern is not unique to IPv6. Any time the same identifier is reused across unrelated activities, it becomes possible to correlate those activities. For example, a network observer can track which destinations a host communicates with and at what times.

In IPv4, when an address changes, the entire address typically changes. But in IPv6, the interface identifier portion can remain constant even as the topological prefix changes. A mobile device moving between a home network and an office network would keep the same interface identifier in its addresses, allowing trackers to follow its movement via a hardware serial number embedded in the address.

Even when upper-layer payloads are encrypted, IP addresses appear in cleartext packet headers and cannot be easily hidden from eavesdroppers. This makes address-based tracking particularly concerning.
sections.eli5: The same part of your address always stays the same, so even if you go to different networks, someone watching can recognize you.

sections.title: Temporary Addresses
sections.content:
The solution is for devices to generate and use temporary addresses alongside their public (permanent) addresses. When a device learns a new network prefix via router advertisement, it creates both a public address and a temporary address from that prefix.

The temporary address uses a randomized interface identifier instead of the permanent one. The device prefers temporary addresses for outgoing connections but keeps the public address for services that need a stable, DNS-registered address. Both types of addresses can receive incoming traffic.

Temporary addresses have limited lifetimes. A preferred lifetime (default one day) determines when the address stops being preferred for new connections. A valid lifetime (default one week) determines when the address expires entirely. When a preferred lifetime expires, a new temporary address is generated with a fresh randomized interface identifier.
sections.eli5: Your device makes a new throw-away address for each day, one that nobody can guess. Meanwhile it keeps a permanent address for things that need stability.

sections.title: Generating and Changing Addresses
sections.content:
When stable storage is available, the device maintains a history value, a 64-bit state saved across restarts. To generate a randomized interface identifier, the device appends its permanent interface identifier to the history value and computes an MD5 hash. The leftmost 64 bits of the hash become the new interface identifier. The rightmost 64 bits become the new history value for the next iteration.

The device performs duplicate address detection (DAD) on each new temporary address to ensure it is not already in use. If DAD detects a collision, a new randomized interface identifier is generated and the process repeats up to five times.

The frequency of address regeneration depends on how the device is used and user privacy preferences. The document recommends generating new addresses at least once per day, with the default preferred lifetime of one day, to make collecting correlated information expensive.
sections.eli5: The device mixes its real hardware address with a random number, uses a special math function to make a fake address, and checks that nobody is using it yet. Then it picks a new random number for tomorrow.

sections.title: Trade-offs and Implications
sections.content:
Privacy improvements come with operational costs. Devices using temporary addresses become harder to debug because a single host will use many addresses over time. Some servers refuse access to clients without a valid reverse DNS name, and temporary addresses may not be registered in DNS.

Administrators may wish to disable temporary addresses in some environments, such as corporate networks where device tracking is acceptable or where operational debugging is important. Implementations should allow administrators and users to configure address generation frequency and policy.
sections.eli5: The downside is that network administrators have a harder time fixing problems when devices keep changing their address.
